Appendix D Guarantees for SFT-Sharpening with Adaptive Sampling

SFT-Sharpening is a simple and natural self-training scheme, and converges to a sharpened policy as n,N→∞n,N\to\infty. However, using a fixed response sample size NN may be wasteful for prompts where the model is confident. To this end, in this section we introduce and analyze, a variant of SFT-Sharpening based on adaptive sampling, which adjusts the number of sampled responses adaptively.

Algorithm

We present the adaptive SFT-Sharpening algorithm only for the special case of the maximum likelihood sharpening self-reward. Let a stopping parameter μ>0\mu>0 be given. For xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}, and yi,1,yi,2…∼πbase(⋅∣xi)y_{i,1},y_{i,2}\ldots\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x_{i}), define a stopping time (e.g., Benjamini and Hochberg (1995)) via:

Nμ​(xi):=inf{k:1max1≤j≤k⁡πbase​(yi,j∣xi)≤kμ}.\displaystyle N_{\mu}(x_{i}):=\inf\left\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq j\leq k}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i,j}\mid{}x_{i})}\leq\frac{k}{\mu}\right\}. (32)

The adaptive SFT-Sharpening algorithm computes adaptively sampled responses yiAdaBoNy^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i} via

yiAdaBoN∼arg​max{logπbase(yi,j∣xi)∣yi,1,…,yi,Nμ​(xi)},y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i}\sim\argmax\left\{\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i,j}\mid{}x_{i})\mid{}y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,N_{\mu}(x_{i})}\right\}, (33)

then trains the sharpened model through SFT:

π^AdaBoN=arg​maxπ∈Π∑i=1nlogπ(yiAdaBoN∣xi).\widehat{\pi}^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}=\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\pi(y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{i}\mid{}x_{i}). (34)

Critically, by using scheme in Eq. 32, this algorithm can stop sampling responses for the prompt xix_{i} if it becomes clear that the confidence is large.

Theoretical guarantee

We now show that adaptive SFT-Sharpening enjoys provable benefits over its non-adaptive counterpart through the dependence on the accuracy parameter ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Given x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and y1,y2​…∼πbase​(x)y_{1},y_{2}\ldots\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x), let Nμ​(x):=infb​i​g​{k:1max1≤i≤k⁡πbase​(yi∣x)≤k/μ​b​i​g}N_{\mu}(x):=\inf big\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i}\mid{}x)}\leq k/\mu big\}, and define a random variable yAdaBoN(x)∼arg​max{logπbase(yi∣x)∣y1,…,yNμ∼πbase(x)}y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}(x)\sim\argmax\left\{\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y_{i}\mid{}x)\mid{}y_{1},\ldots,y_{N_{\mu}}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)\right\}. Let πμAdaBoN​(x)\pi^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{\mu}(x) denote the distribution over yAdaBoN​(x)y^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}(x). We make the following realizability assumption. {assumption} The model class Π\Pi satisfies πμAdaBoN∈Π\pi^{\texttt{AdaBoN}}_{\mu}\in\Pi. Compared to SFT-Sharpening, we require a somewhat stronger coverage coefficient given by

\macc@depth​Δ​\macc@set@skewchar​\macc@nested@a​111​Ccov=𝔼x∼μ⁡[1maxy∈𝒴⁡πbase​(y∣x)].\displaystyle\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}=\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right]. (35)

Appendix E Computational and Representational Challenges in Sharpening

In this section, we make several basic observations about the inherent computational and representational challenges of maximum-likelihood sharpening. First, in Section E.1, we focus on computational challenges, and show that computing a sharpened response for a given prompt xx can be computationally intractable in general, even when sampling y∼πbase(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}x) can be performed efficiently. Then, in Section E.2, we shift our focus to representational challenges, and show that even if πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} is an autoregressive model, the “sharpened” version of πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} may not be representable as an autoregressive model with the same architecture. These results motivate the statistical assumptions (coverage and realizability) made in our analysis of SFT-Sharpening and RLHF-Sharpening in Section 4.

To make the results in this section precise, we work in perhaps the simplest special case of autoregressive language modelling, where the model class consists of multi-layer linear softmax models. Formally, let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the space of prompts, and let 𝒴:=𝒱H\mathcal{Y}:=\mathcal{V}^{H} be the space of responses, where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the vocabulary space and HH is the horizon. For a collection of fixed/known dd-dimensional feature mappings ϕh:𝒳×𝒱h→ℝd\phi_{h}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{V}^{h}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} and a norm parameter BB, we define the model class Πϕ,B,H\Pi_{\phi,B,H} as the set of models

πθ(y1:H∣x)=∏h=1Hπθh(yh∣x,y1:h−1)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x)=\prod_{h=1}^{H}\pi_{\theta_{h}}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1}) (39)

where

πθ(yh∣x,y1:h−1)∝exp(⟨ϕ(x,y1:h),θh⟩)\pi_{\theta}(y_{h}\mid{}x,y_{1:h-1})\propto\exp(\langle\phi(x,y_{1:h}),\theta_{h}\rangle) (40)

and θ=(θ1,…,θH)∈(ℝd)H\theta=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{H})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{H} is any tuple with ∥θh∥2≤B\lVert\theta_{h}\rVert_{2}\leq B for all h∈[H]h\in[H].

Given query access to ϕ\phi, for any given parameter vector θ\theta and prompt xx, sampling from a linear softmax model πθ\pi_{\theta} (Eq. 39) is computationally tractable, since it only requires time poly⁡(H,|𝒱|,d)\mathrm{poly}(H,|\mathcal{V}|,d). Similarly, evaluating πθ(y1:H∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x) for given prompt xx and response y1:Hy_{1:H} is computationally tractable. However, the following proposition shows that computing the sharpened response arg​maxy1:H∈𝒱Hπθ(y1:H∣x)\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}x) for a given parameter θ\theta and response xx is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard. Hence, even inference-time sharpening is computationally intractable in the worst case.

Then among y1:Hy_{1:H} with yH−1=yH=1y_{H-1}=y_{H}=1, 2H−2⋅πθ(y1:H∣⟂)2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp) is maximized when y1:H−2y_{1:H-2} corresponds to a max-cut in GG. If GG has an odd number of edges, then some max-cut removes strictly more than half of the edges, and for the corresponding sequence y1:Hy_{1:H} we have 2H−2⋅πθ(y1:H∣⟂)≥(1/2+Ω(1))⋅(1−exp(−Ω(B)))2^{H-2}\cdot\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\geq(1/2+\Omega(1))\cdot(1-\exp(-\Omega(B))), which is greater than 1/21/2 when we take B:=HB:=H and HH is sufficiently large. Thus, computing arg​maxy1:H∈𝒱Hπθ(y1:H∣⟂)\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp) yields a max-cut of GG. It is well-known that computing a max-cut in a graph is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard, and the assumption that GG has an odd number of edges is without loss of generality. ∎

E.2 Representational Challenges

To give provable guarantees for our sharpening algorithms, we required certain realizability assumptions, which in particular posited that the model class actually contains a “sharpened” version of πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} (Sections 4.1 and 4.2.1). In the simple example of a single-layer linear softmax model classes (corresponding to H=1H=1 in the above definition), Section 4.2.1 is in fact satisfied, and the sharpened model can be obtained by increasing the temperature of πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}}. However, multi-layer linear softmax models with H≫1H\gg 1 are more realistic. The following proposition shows that as soon as H≥2H\geq 2, multi-layer linear softmax model classes may not be closed under sharpening. This illustrates a potential drawback of training-time sharpening compared to inference-time sharpening, which requires no realizability assumptions. It also provides a simple example where greedy decoding does not yield a sequence-level arg-max response (since increasing temperature in a multi-layer softmax model class exactly converges to the greedy decoding).

{proposition}

Let 𝒳={⟂}\mathcal{X}=\{\perp\}, 𝒱=[n]\mathcal{V}=[n], and H=d=2H=d=2. For any nn sufficiently large, there is a multi-layer linear softmax policy class Πϕ,B,H\Pi_{\phi,B,H} and a policy πbase∈Πϕ,B,H\pi_{\texttt{base}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B,H} such that y1:H⋆:=arg​maxy1:H∈𝒱Hπθ(y1:H∣⟂)y^{\star}_{1:H}:=\argmax_{y_{1:H}\in\mathcal{V}^{H}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{1:H}\mid{}\perp) is unique, but for all B′>BB^{\prime}>B and π∈Πϕ,B′,H\pi\in\Pi_{\phi,B^{\prime},H}, it holds that π(y1:H⋆∣⟂)≤1/2\pi(y^{\star}_{1:H}\mid{}\perp)\leq 1/2.

Proof of Section E.2. Throughout, we omit the dependence on the prompt ⟂\perp for notational clarity. Since H=2H=2, the model class consists of models πθ\pi_{\theta} of the form

πθ(a)=πθ1(y1)πθ2(y2∣y1)=exp⁡(⟨ϕ1​(y1),θ1⟩)Zθ1exp(⟨ϕ2(y1:2),θ2⟩)Zθ2​(y1)\pi_{\theta}(a)=\pi_{\theta_{1}}(y_{1})\pi_{\theta_{2}}(y_{2}\mid{}y_{1})=\frac{\exp(\langle\phi_{1}(y_{1}),\theta_{1}\rangle)}{Z_{\theta_{1}}}\frac{\exp(\langle\phi_{2}(y_{1:2}),\theta_{2}\rangle)}{Z_{\theta_{2}}(y_{1})}\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:softmax-h2} (42)

for Zθ1:=∑y1∈𝒱exp⁡(⟨ϕ1​(y1),θ1⟩)Z_{\theta_{1}}\vcentcolon={}\sum_{y_{1}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\langle\phi_{1}(y_{1}),\theta_{1}\rangle) and Zθ2(y1):=∑y2∈𝒱exp(⟨ϕ2(y1:2),θ2⟩)Z_{\theta_{2}}(y_{1})\vcentcolon={}\sum_{y_{2}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\langle\phi_{2}(y_{1:2}),\theta_{2}\rangle).

Define ϕ1\phi_{1} by:

ϕ1​(i)={e1 if ​i=1e1 if ​i=2e2 if ​i≥3.\phi_{1}(i)=\begin{cases}e_{1}&\text{ if }i=1\\ e_{1}&\text{ if }i=2\\ e_{2}&\text{ if }i\geq 3\end{cases}. (43)

Define ϕ2\phi_{2} by:

ϕ2​(i,j)={e1 if ​i=2,j=1e2 if ​i=2,j≠10 if ​i≠2.\phi_{2}(i,j)=\begin{cases}e_{1}&\text{ if }i=2,j=1\\ e_{2}&\text{ if }i=2,j\neq 1\\ 0&\text{ if }i\neq 2\end{cases}. (44)

Define πbase:=πθ⋆\pi_{\texttt{base}}:=\pi_{\theta^{\star}} where θ1⋆:=θ2⋆:=B⋅e1\theta^{\star}_{1}:=\theta^{\star}_{2}:=B\cdot{}e_{1} for a parameter B≥log⁡(n)B\geq\log(n). Then πbase​(1)=πbase​(2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1)=\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2) and πbase​(i)≤e−B​πbase​(2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(i)\leq e^{-B}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2) for all i∈{3,…,n}i\in\{3,\dots,n\}. Moreover, πbase(⋅∣i)=𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿([n])\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid{}i)=\mathsf{Unif}([n]) for all i≠2i\neq 2, and πbase​(j∣2)≤e−B​πbase​(1∣2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(j\mid{}2)\leq e^{-B}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1\mid{}2) for all j≠1j\neq 1. Thus,

πbase​(2,1)=πbase​(2)​πbase​(1∣2)≥12+(n−2)​e−B⋅11+(n−1)​e−B≥Ω⁡(1)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2,1)=\pi_{\texttt{base}}(2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(1\mid{}2)\geq\frac{1}{2+(n-2)e^{-B}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+(n-1)e^{-B}}\geq\Omega(1) (45)

whereas πbase​(i,j)=O⁡(1/n)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(i,j)=O(1/n) for all (i,j)≠(2,1)(i,j)\neq(2,1). Thus, (2,1)(2,1) is the sequence-level argmax for sufficiently large nn. However, for any πθ\pi_{\theta} of the form described in Eq. 42, we have

πθ​(2,1)≤πθ​(2)≤πθ​(2)πθ​(1)+πθ​(2)=12\pi_{\theta}(2,1)\leq\pi_{\theta}(2)\leq\frac{\pi_{\theta}(2)}{\pi_{\theta}(1)+\pi_{\theta}(2)}=\frac{1}{2} (46)

since ϕ⁡(1)=ϕ⁡(2)\phi(1)=\phi(2). This means that there is no B′B^{\prime} for which Πϕ,B′,H\Pi_{\phi,B^{\prime},H} contains an (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-sharpened policy for πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} for any δ>1/2\delta>1/2. ∎

Part II Proofs

Appendix F Preliminaries

F.1 Guarantees for Approximate Maximizers

Recall that the theoretical guarantees for sharpening algorithms in Section 4 provide convergence to the set 𝒚⋆​(x):=arg​maxy∈𝒴⁡πbase​(y∣x)\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\vcentcolon={}\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x) of (potentially non-unique) maximizers for the maximum-likelihood sharpening self-reward function log⁡πbase​(y∣x)\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x). These guarantees require that the base model πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} places sufficient provability mass on 𝒚⋆​(x)\bm{y}^{\star}(x), which may not always be realistic. To address this, throughout this appendix we state and prove more general versions of our theoretical results that allow for approximate maximizers, and consequently enjoy weaker coverage assumptions

For a parameter γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) we define

𝒚γ⋆​(x):={y∣πbase​(y∣x)≥(1−γ)⋅maxy∈𝒴⁡πbase​(y∣x)}\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\vcentcolon={}\left\{y\mid{}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)\geq{}(1-\gamma)\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\right\} (47)

as the set of (1−γ)(1-\gamma)-approximate maximizers for log⁡πbase​(y∣x)\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x). We quantify the quality of a sharpened model as follows. {definition}[Sharpened model] We say that a model π^\widehat{\pi} is (ϵ,δ,γ)(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)-sharpened relative to πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} if

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≥1−δ]≥1−ϵ.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}\left(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x\right)\geq{}1-\delta\right]\geq{}1-\epsilon. (48)

That is, an (ϵ,δ,γ)(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)-sharpened policy places at least 1−δ1-\delta mass on (1−γ)(1-\gamma)-approximate arg-max responses on all but an ϵ\epsilon-fraction of prompts under μ\mu.

Lastly, we will make use of the following generalized coverage coefficient

Ccov,γ=𝔼x∼μ⁡[1πbase​(𝐲γ⋆​(x)∣x)],\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}=\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right], (49)

which has Ccov,γ≤CcovC_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}\leq{}C_{\texttt{cov}}.

Appendix G Proofs from Section 3.1

Proof of Section 3.1. We prove the result by induction. Fix x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and let y1⋆,…,yH⋆:=y⋆​(x)y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\vcentcolon={}y^{\star}(x). Fix h∈[H]h\in[H], and assume by induction that y^h′=yh′⋆\widehat{y}_{h^{\prime}}=y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}} for all h′<hh^{\prime}<h. We claim that in this case,

πh​(yh⋆∣y^1,…,y^h−1,x)=πh​(yh⋆∣y1⋆,…,yh−1⋆,x)>1/2,\displaystyle\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}\widehat{y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{y}_{h-1},x)=\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x)>1/2, (69)

which implies that y^h=yh⋆\widehat{y}_{h}=y^{\star}_{h}. To see this, we observe that by Bayes’ rule,

π⁡(y1⋆,…,yH⋆∣x)\displaystyle\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\mid{}x) ≤π⁡(y1⋆,…,yh⋆∣x)\displaystyle\leq{}\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}x) (70)
=∏h′=1hπh′​(yh′⋆∣y1⋆,…,yh′−1⋆,x)≤πh​(yh⋆∣y1⋆,…,yh−1⋆,x).\displaystyle=\prod_{h^{\prime}=1}^{h}\pi_{h^{\prime}}(y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h^{\prime}-1},x)\leq{}\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x). (71)

If we were to have πh​(yh⋆∣y^1,…,y^h−1,x)=πh​(yh⋆∣y1⋆,…,yh−1⋆,x)≤1/2\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}\widehat{y}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{y}_{h-1},x)=\pi_{h}(y^{\star}_{h}\mid{}y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{h-1},x)\leq{}1/2, it would contradict the assumption that π⁡(y1⋆,…,yH⋆∣x)>1/2\pi(y^{\star}_{1},\ldots,y^{\star}_{H}\mid{}x)>1/2. This proves the result. ∎

Appendix H Proofs from Section 3.3

Below, we state and prove a generalization of Sections 3.3 and D which allows for approximate maximizers in the sense of Section F.1, as well as a more general coverage coefficient.

To state the result, for a model π\pi, we define

𝒚γπ​(x)={y∣π⁡(y∣x)≥(1−γ)⋅maxy∈𝒴⁡π⁡(y∣x)}.\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\pi}_{\gamma}(x)=\left\{y\mid{}\pi(y\mid{}x)\geq{}(1-\gamma)\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi(y\mid x)\right\}. (72)

with the convention that Ccov,γ,p=Ccov,γ,p​(πbase)C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}=C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi_{\texttt{base}}). Our most general lower bound, Appendix H, holds in the regime where γ=1/2\gamma=1/2, and thus the best responseyy has bounded margin away from suboptimal responses. {theorem}[Lower bound for sharpening] Fix integers d≥1d\geq 1 and p≥1p\geq 1 and parameters ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) and C≥1C\geq 1, and set γ=1/2\gamma=1/2. There exists a class of models Π\Pi such that i) log|Π|≍d(1+log(Cϵ−1/p))\log|\Pi|\asymp d(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p})), ii) supπ∈ΠCcov,γ,p​(π)≲C\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)\lesssim C, and iii) 𝒚γπ​(x)\bm{y}^{\pi}_{\gamma}(x) is a singleton for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, for which any sharpening algorithm π^\widehat{\pi} that attains 𝔼[ℙx∼μ[π^(𝐲γπbase(x))>1/2]]≥1−ϵ\En\left[\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}_{\gamma}(x))>1/2]\right]\geq 1-\epsilon for all πbase∈Π\pi_{\texttt{base}}\in\Pi must collect a total number of samples m=n⋅Nm=n\cdot{}N at least

m≳{C​log⁡|Π|ϵ1+1/p(1+log(Cϵ−1/p))sample-and-evaluate oracle,C​log⁡|Π|ϵ1/p(1+log(Cϵ−1/p))adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle.\displaystyle m\gtrsim\begin{cases}\frac{C\log|\Pi|}{\epsilon^{1+1/p}(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p}))}&\text{sample-and-evaluate oracle},\\ \frac{C\log|\Pi|}{\epsilon^{1/p}(1+\log(C\epsilon^{-1/p}))}&\text{adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle}.\end{cases} (74)
Proof of Appendix H

Let parameters d,p∈ℕd,p\in\mathbb{N} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be given, and set γ=1/2\gamma=1/2. Let M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N} and Δ>0\Delta>0 be parameters to be chosen later. Let 𝒳={x0,x1,…,xd}\mathcal{X}=\{x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{d}\} and 𝒴={y0,y1,…,yM}\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{0},y_{1},\dots,y_{M}\} be arbitrary discrete sets (with |𝒳|=d+1\lvert\mathcal{X}\rvert=d+1 and |𝒴|=M+1\lvert\mathcal{Y}\rvert=M+1).

Construction of prompt distribution and model class

We use the same construction for the non-adaptive and adaptive lower bounds in the theorem statement. We define the prompt distribution μ\mu via

μ:=(1−Δ)​δx0+Δd​∑i=1dδxi,\displaystyle\mu:=(1-\Delta)\updelta_{x_{0}}+\frac{\Delta}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\updelta_{x_{i}}, (75)

where δx\updelta_{x} denotes the Dirac delta distribution on element xx.

As the first step toward constructing the model class Π\Pi, we introduce a family of distributions (P0,P1,…,PM)(P_{0},P_{1},\dots,P_{M}) on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} as follows

P0=δy0,∀i≥1,Pi=1(1−γ)​M​δyi+∑j∈[M]∖{i}1M​(1−γ(M−1)​(1−γ))​δyj.\displaystyle P_{0}=\updelta_{y_{0}},\quad\forall i\geq 1,~P_{i}=\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)M}\updelta_{y_{i}}+\sum_{j\in[M]\setminus\{i\}}\frac{1}{M}\left(1-\frac{\gamma}{(M-1)(1-\gamma)}\right)\updelta_{y_{j}}. (76)

Next, for or any index ℐ=(j1,j2,…,jd)∈[M]d\mathcal{I}=(j_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{d})\in[M]^{d}, define a model

πℐ​(xi)={P0i=0Pjii>0.\displaystyle\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(x_{i})=\begin{cases}P_{0}&i=0\\ P_{j_{i}}&i>0\end{cases}. (77)

We define the model class as

Π:={πℐ:ℐ∈[M]d},\displaystyle\Pi:=\{\pi^{\mathcal{I}}:\mathcal{I}\in[M]^{d}\}, (78)

which we note has

log⁡|Π|\displaystyle\log|\Pi| =d​log⁡M.\displaystyle=d\log M. (79)
Preliminary technical results

Define

𝒚γℐ​(x):={y:πℐ​(y∣x)≥(1−γ)​maxy∈𝒴​πℐ​(y∣x)}.\displaystyle\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x):=\{y:\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid x)\geq(1-\gamma)\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x)\}. (80)

The following property is immediate. {lemma} Let ℐ=(j1,…,jd)∈[d]M\mathcal{I}=(j_{1},\dots,j_{d})\in[d]^{M}. Then 𝒚γℐ​(xi)={yji}\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}}\} if i>0i>0, and 𝒚γℐ​(x0)={y0}\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{0})=\{y_{0}\}. In view of this result, we define yℐ​(x)=arg​maxy⁡πℐ​(y∣x)y^{\mathcal{I}}(x)=\argmax_{y}\pi^{\mathcal{I}}(y\mid{}x) as the unique arg-max response for xx.

Going forward, let us fix the algorithm under consideration. Let ℙℐ​[⋅]\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot] denote the law over the dataset used by the algorithm when the true instance is πℐ\pi^{\mathcal{I}} (including possible randomness and adaptivity from the algorithm itself), and let 𝔼ℐ⁡[⋅]\En^{\mathcal{I}}[\cdot] denote the corresponding expectation. The following lemma is a basic technical result. {lemma}[Reduction to classification] Let π^\widehat{\pi} be the model produced by an algorithm with access to a (adaptive) sample-and-evaluate oracle for πℐ\pi^{\mathcal{I}}. Suppose that for some ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq{}0,

𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐℙx∼μ[π^(𝐲γℐ(x)∣x)>1/2]≥1−ϵ.\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon. (81)

Define ℐ^=(j^1,…,j^d)\widehat{\mathcal{I}}=(\widehat{j}_{1},\dots,\widehat{j}_{d}) via j^i=arg​maxj⁡π^​(yj∣xi)\widehat{j}_{i}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i}), and write ℐ=(j1⋆,…,jd⋆)\mathcal{I}=(j_{1}^{\star},\dots,j_{d}^{\star}). Then,

1d∑i=1d𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐ[𝕀{j^i≠ji⋆}]≤ϵ/Δ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\epsilon/\Delta. (82)

Proof of Appendix H. As established in Appendix H, under instance ℐ\mathcal{I}, 𝒚γℐ​(xi)={yji⋆}\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i})=\{y_{j_{i}^{\star}}\} for any i∈[d]i\in[d]. Thus, whenever π^​(𝒚γℐ​(xi))>1/2\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x_{i}))>1/2, ji⋆=arg​maxj⁡π^​(yj∣xi)=:j^ij_{i}^{\star}=\argmax_{j}\widehat{\pi}(y_{j}\mid x_{i})=:\widehat{j}_{i}. The result follows by noting that the event {∃i∈[d]:x=xi}\{\exists i\in[d]:x=x_{i}\} occurs with probability at least Δ\Delta under x∼μx\sim\mu. ∎

Lower bound under sample-and-evaluate oracle

Recall that in the non-adaptive framework, the sample complexity mm is fixed. In light of Appendix H, it suffices to establishes the following claim. {lemma} There exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that for all M≥8M\geq 8, if m≤c​d​M/Δm\leq cdM/\Delta, then 𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐ[𝕀{j^i≠ji⋆}]≥1/8\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\geq 1/8 for all ii. With this, the result follows by selecting Δ=16​ϵ\Delta=16\epsilon, with which Appendix H implies that any algorithm with 𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐℙx∼μ[π^(𝐲γℐ(x)∣x)>1/2]≥1−ϵ\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)>1/2]\geq{}1-\epsilon must have m≳d​M/Δm\gtrsim dM/\Delta. To conclude, we choose M≍1+Cϵ−1/pM\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p}, which gives m≍d​M/Δ≍d​C​ϵ−(1+1/p)≍ϵ−(1+1/p)​log⁡Π/log⁡(1+C​ϵ1/p)m\asymp dM/\Delta\asymp dC\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\asymp\epsilon^{-(1+1/p)}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p}). Finally, we check that with this choice, all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi satisfy

Ccov,γ,p​(π)\displaystyle C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi) =(ℙx∼μ[x=x0]+(M(1−γ))pℙx∼μ[x≠x0])1/p\displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x=x_{0}\right]+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\neq x_{0}\right]\right)^{1/p} (83)
=((1−Δ)+(M⁡(1−γ))p​Δ)1/p\displaystyle=\left((1-\Delta)+\left(M(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\Delta\right)^{1/p} (84)
≲((1−Δ)+(8​C​(1−γ))p)1/p≲C.\displaystyle\lesssim\left((1-\Delta)+\left(8C(1-\gamma)\right)^{p}\right)^{1/p}\lesssim C. (85)

ℙ[mi≤2Δm/d]≥12\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d]\geq\frac{1}{2} (86)

=𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐ[𝕀{ℰi}𝔼ℐ∼ℙ[ℐ=⋅∣𝒟][𝕀{j^i≠ji⋆}]],\displaystyle=\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\mathcal{E}_{i}\}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{I}=\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}]}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j^{\star}_{i}\}\right]\right], (88)

≥14​𝔼ℐ∼Unif​ℙℐ​[ℰi∣mi≤2​Δ​m/d],\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{i}\mid m_{i}\leq 2\Delta m/d\right], (90)

Lower bound under adaptive sample-and-evaluate oracle

In the adaptive framework, we let mim_{i} denote the (potentially random) number of tuples (x,y,log⁡πbase​(y∣x))(x,y,\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)) observed by the algorithm in which x=xix=x_{i}. Note that unlike the non-adaptive framework, the distribution over mim_{i} depends on the underlying instance ℐ\mathcal{I} with which the algorithm interacts.

To begin, from Appendix H and Markov’s inequality, if π^\widehat{\pi} satisfies the guarantee 𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐℙx∼μ[π^(𝐲γℐ(x))>1/2]≥1−ϵ\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\mathcal{I}}_{\gamma}(x))>1/2]\geq 1-\epsilon, then there exists a set of indices Sgood⊂[d]S_{\texttt{good}}\subset[d] such that1414 14 We emphasize that the set SgoodS_{\texttt{good}} is not a random variable, and depends only on the algorithm itself.

|Sgood|≥⌊d/2⌋,∀i∈Sgood,𝔼ℐ∼Unif𝔼ℐ[𝕀{j^i≠ji⋆}]≤2​ϵΔ.\displaystyle|S_{\texttt{good}}|\geq\lfloor d/2\rfloor,\quad\forall i\in S_{\texttt{good}},~\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{j}_{i}\neq j_{i}^{\star}\}\right]\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{\Delta}. (92)

We now appeal to the following lemma. {lemma} As long as M≥6M\geq{}6, it holds that for all i∈[d]i\in[d],

Combining Appendix H with Eq. 92, it follows that there exist absolute constant c1,c2,c3>0c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0 such that if Δ=c1⋅ϵ\Delta=c_{1}\cdot{}\epsilon, then for all i∈Sgoodi\in S_{\texttt{good}},

𝔼ℐ∼Unifℙℐ[mi≥c2M]≥c3.\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\geq{}c_{2}M\right]\geq{}c_{3}. (94)

Thus, with this choice for Δ\Delta, we have that i∈Sgoodi\in S_{\texttt{good}},

𝔼ℐ∼Unif⁡𝔼ℐ⁡[mi]≳M,\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m_{i}\right]\gtrsim M, (95)

and we can lower bound the algorithm’s expected sample complexity by summing over i∈Sgoodi\in S_{\texttt{good}}:

𝔼ℐ∼Unif⁡𝔼ℐ⁡[m]≥𝔼ℐ∼Unif⁡𝔼ℐ⁡[∑i∈Sgoodmi]≳|Sgood|​M≳dM.\displaystyle\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[m\right]\geq\En_{\mathcal{I}\sim\texttt{Unif}}\En^{\mathcal{I}}\left[\sum_{i\in S_{\texttt{good}}}m_{i}\right]\gtrsim|S_{\texttt{good}}|M\gtrsim dM. (96)

The result now follows by tuning M≍1+Cϵ−1/pM\asymp 1+C\epsilon^{-1/p} as in the proof of the lower bound for non-adaptive sampling, which gives 𝔼[m]≳dM≍dCϵ−1/p≍ϵ−1/plogΠ/log(1+Cϵ1/p)\En[m]\gtrsim{}dM\asymp dC\epsilon^{-1/p}\asymp\epsilon^{-1/p}\log\Pi/\log(1+C\epsilon^{1/p}) and Ccov,γ,p​(π)≲CC_{\texttt{cov},\gamma,p}(\pi)\lesssim{}C for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi.

Appendix I Proofs from Section 4.1 and Appendix D

The following theorem is a generalization of Section 4.1 which allows for approximate maximizers in the sense of Section F.1. {theorem} Let ρ,δ∈(0,1)\rho,\delta\in(0,1) be given, and suppose we set N=N⋆​log⁡(2​δ−1)N=N^{\star}\log(2\delta^{-1}) for a parameter N⋆∈ℕN^{\star}\in\mathbb{N}. Then for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, SFT-Sharpening ensures that with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho, for any γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), the output model π^\widehat{\pi} satisfies

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−2δ]≲1δ⋅log⁡(|Π|​ρ−1)n+Ccov,γN⋆.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-2\delta\right]\lesssim{}\frac{1}{\delta}\cdot{}\frac{\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})}{n}+\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{N^{\star}}. (105)

In particular, given (ϵ,δ,γ)(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma), by setting n=C4.1​log⁡|Π|δ​ϵn=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{\log\lvert\Pi\rvert}{\delta\epsilon} and N⋆=C4.1​Ccov,γϵN^{\star}=C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{\epsilon} for a sufficiently large absolute constant C4.1>0C_{\ref{thm:bestofn}}>0, we are guaranteed that

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ]≤ϵ.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\leq\epsilon. (106)

The total sample complexity is

m=O⁡(Ccov,γ​log⁡(|Π|​ρ−1)​log⁡(δ−1)δ​ϵ2).\displaystyle m=O\left(\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})\log(\delta^{-1})}{\delta\epsilon^{2}}\right). (107)

Proof of Appendix I. Under realizability of πNBoN\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N} (Section 4.1), Section F.2 implies that the output of SFT-Sharpening satisfies, with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

𝔼x∼μ[D𝖧2(π^(⋅∣x),πNBoN(⋅∣x))]≤εstat2:=2​log⁡(|Π|/ρ)n.\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}\vcentcolon={}\frac{2\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert/\rho)}{n}. (108)

Henceforth we condition on the event that Eq. 108 holds. Let

𝒳good:={x∈𝒳∣N⋆≥1πbase​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)}\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\vcentcolon={}\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid N^{\star}\geq\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right\} (109)

denote the set of prompts for which πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} places sufficiently high mass on 𝒚γ⋆​(x)\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x). We can bound

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right] (110)
≤ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ,x∈𝒳good]+ℙx∼μ[x∉𝒳good].\displaystyle\qquad\leq{}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta,x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right]+\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\notin\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right]. (111)

To bound the first term in Eq. 111, note that if x∈𝒳goodx\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}, then πNBoN​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)≥1−δ/2\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\geq{}1-\delta/2. Indeed, observe that y∼πNBoN(⋅∣x)∉𝒚γ⋆(x)y\sim\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\notin\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x) if and only if y1,…,yN∼πbase​(x)y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x) have yi∉𝒚γ⋆​(x)y_{i}\notin\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x) for all ii, which happens with probability (1−πbase​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x))N≤(1−1/N⋆)N≤δ/2(1-\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x))^{N}\leq(1-1/N^{\star})^{N}\leq\delta/2 since x∈𝒳goodx\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}. It follows that for any such xx, we can lower bound (using the data processing inequality)

D𝖧2(π^(⋅∣x),πNBoN(⋅∣x))\displaystyle D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right) ≥(1−π^​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)−1−πNBoN​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x))2\displaystyle\geq\left(\sqrt{1-\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}-\sqrt{1-\pi^{\texttt{BoN}}_{N}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right)^{2} (112)
≳δ⋅𝕀{π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ}.\displaystyle\gtrsim{}\delta\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right\}. (113)

By Eqs. 108 and 113, it follows that

ℙx∼μ​[π^​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)≤1−δ,x∈𝒳good]≲εstat2δ.\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta,x\in\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right]\lesssim\frac{\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}}{\delta}. (114)

For the second term in Eq. 111, we bound

ℙx∼μ[x∉𝒳good]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[x\notin\mathcal{X}_{\texttt{good}}\right] =ℙx∼μ[N⋆<1πbase​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[N^{\star}<\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right] (115)
=ℙx∼μ[1N⋆​πbase​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)>1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{N^{\star}\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}>1\right] (116)
≤1N⋆​𝔼x∼μ​[1πbase​(𝐲γ⋆​(x)∣x)]\displaystyle\leq{}\frac{1}{N^{\star}}\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)}\right] (117)
≤Ccov,γN⋆\displaystyle\leq{}\frac{C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}}{N^{\star}} (118)

via Markov’s inequality and the definition of Ccov,γC_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}. Substituting both bounds into Eq. 111 completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Appendix D. The proof begins similarly to Section 4.1. By realizability of πNμ\pi_{N_{\mu}}, Section F.2 implies that the output of SFT-Sharpening satisfies, with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

𝔼x∼μ[D𝖧2(π^(⋅∣x),πNμ(⋅∣x))]≤εstat2:=2​log⁡(|Π|/ρ)n.\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\right]\leq\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}\vcentcolon={}\frac{2\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert/\rho)}{n}. (119)

Condition on the event that this guarantee holds. We invoke the following lemma, proven in the sequel. {lemma} Let PP be a distribution on a discrete space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Let 𝒚⋆=arg​maxy∈𝒴⁡P​(y)\bm{y}^{\star}=\argmax_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}P(y) and let P⋆:=maxy∈𝒴⁡P⁡(y)P^{\star}:=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}P(y). Let y1,y2,…∼Py_{1},y_{2},\ldots\sim{}P, and for any stopping time τ\tau, define

y^τ∈arg​max⁡{P⁡(y):y∈{y1,…,yτ}}.\displaystyle\widehat{y}_{\tau}\in\argmax\left\{P(y):y\in\left\{y_{1},\dots,y_{\tau}\right\}\right\}. (120)

Next, for a parameter μ>0\mu>0, define the stopping time

Nμ:=inf{k:1max1≤i≤k⁡P⁡(yi)≤k/μ}.\displaystyle N_{\mu}:=\inf\left\{k:\frac{1}{\max_{1\leq i\leq k}P(y_{i})}\leq k/\mu\right\}. (121)

Then

𝔼⁡[Nμ]≤μ+(1/|𝐲⋆|)P⋆.\displaystyle\En[N_{\mu}]\leq\frac{\mu+(1/|\bm{y}^{\star}|)}{P^{\star}}. (122)

In addition, for any stopping time τ≥Nμ\tau\geq N_{\mu} (including τ=Nμ\tau=N_{\mu} itself), we have ℙ[y^τ∉𝒚⋆]≤e−|𝒚⋆|​μ\mathbb{P}[\widehat{y}_{\tau}\notin\bm{y}^{\star}]\leq e^{-\lvert\bm{y}^{\star}\rvert\mu}. This lemma, with our choice of μ\mu, ensures that for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

πNμ​(𝒚⋆​(x)∣x)≥1−e−μ=1−δ/2.\displaystyle\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)\geq 1-e^{-\mu}=1-\delta/2. (123)

Following the reasoning in Eq. 113, this implies that

D𝖧2(π^(⋅∣x),πNμ(⋅∣x))≳δ⋅𝕀{π^(𝒚⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ},\displaystyle D^{2}_{\mathsf{H}}\left(\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid{}x),\pi_{N_{\mu}}(\cdot\mid{}x)\right)\gtrsim{}\delta\cdot\mathbb{I}\left\{\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right\}, (124)

so that

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ]≲εstat2δ\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\lesssim\frac{\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}}{\delta} (125)

as desired.

To bound the expected sample complexity, we observe that

𝔼⁡[m]=n⋅𝔼⁡[Nμ​(x)]​≤(i)​𝔼​[1+μπbase​(𝐲⋆​(x)∣x)]=(1+μ)​\macc@depth​Δ​\macc@set@skewchar​\macc@nested@a​111​Ccov,\displaystyle\En[m]=n\cdot\En[N_{\mu}(x)]\overset{(i)}{\leq}\En\left[\frac{1+\mu}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}\right]=(1+\mu)\macc@depth\char 1\relax\macc@set@skewchar\macc@nested@a 111{C}_{\texttt{cov}}, (126)

where inequality (i)(i) invokes Appendix I once more. ∎

Proof of Appendix I. Define N⋆:=μ/P⋆N^{\star}:=\mu/P^{\star}. To bound the tails of NμN_{\mu}, define

τ=inf{k∣k≥N⋆​ and ​𝒚⋆∩{y1,…,yk}≠∅}.\displaystyle\tau=\inf\{k\mid{}k\geq N^{\star}\text{ and }\bm{y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\neq\varnothing\}. (127)

It follows from the definition that Nμ≤τN_{\mu}\leq\tau, since for any k≥N⋆k\geq{}N^{\star}, if there exists i≤ki\leq{}k such that yi∈𝒚⋆y_{i}\in\bm{y}^{\star}, then

1P⁡(yi)=1P⋆=N⋆μ≤kμ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{P(y_{i})}=\frac{1}{P^{\star}}=\frac{N^{\star}}{\mu}\leq\frac{k}{\mu}. (128)

Thus, for k≥N⋆k\geq N^{\star}, we can bound

ℙ[Nμ>k]≤ℙ[τ>k]=ℙ[𝒴⋆∩{y1,…,yk}=∅]≤(1−|𝒚⋆|P⋆)k,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[N_{\mu}>k]\leq\mathbb{P}[\tau>k]=\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{Y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}=\varnothing]\leq(1-|\bm{y}^{\star}|P^{\star})^{k}, (129)

and consequently

𝔼⁡[Nμ]≤𝔼⁡[τ]\displaystyle\En[N_{\mu}]\leq\En[\tau] ≤𝔼[τ𝕀{τ≤N⋆}]+𝔼[τ𝕀{τ>N⋆}]\displaystyle\leq\En[\tau\mathbb{I}\{\tau\leq N^{\star}\}]+\En[\tau\mathbb{I}\{\tau>N^{\star}\}] (130)
≤N⋆+∑k>N⋆(1−|𝒚⋆|​P⋆)k\displaystyle\leq N^{\star}+\sum_{k>N^{\star}}(1-|\bm{y}^{\star}|P^{\star})^{k} (131)
≤N⋆+1|𝒚⋆|​P​(y⋆)=μ+1/|𝒚⋆|P⁡(y⋆).\displaystyle\leq N^{\star}+\frac{1}{|\bm{y}^{\star}|P(y^{\star})}=\frac{\mu+1/|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P(y^{\star})}. (132)

To prove correctness, observe that Nμ≥N⋆N_{\mu}\geq N^{\star}, because for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, 1P⁡(y)≥N⋆/μ\frac{1}{P(y)}\geq N^{\star}/\mu. Hence, any stopping time τ≥Nμ\tau\geq N_{\mu} also satisfies τ≥N⋆\tau\geq N^{\star}, and moreover has y^τ∈𝒚⋆\widehat{y}_{\tau}\in\bm{y}^{\star} whenever 𝒚⋆∩{y1,y2,…,yτ}≠∅\bm{y}^{\star}\cap\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{\tau}\}\neq\varnothing. This fails to occur with probability no more than

(1−|𝒚⋆|P⋆)N⋆=(1−|𝒚⋆|P⋆)μ/P⋆≤e−|𝒚⋆|​μ.\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P^{\star}}\right)^{N^{\star}}=\left(1-\frac{|\bm{y}^{\star}|}{P^{\star}}\right)^{\mu/P^{\star}}\leq e^{-|\bm{y}^{\star}|\mu}. (133)

J.1 Proof of Section 4.2.1

We state and prove a generalized version of Section 4.2.1. In the assumptions below, we fix a parameter γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1); the setting γ=0\gamma=0 corresponds to Section 4.2.1.

{assumption}

[Coverage] All π∈Π\pi\in\Pi satisfy 𝒞π≤Cconc\mathcal{C}_{\pi}\leq C_{\texttt{conc}} for a parameter Cconc≥(1−γ)−1​Ccov,γC_{\texttt{conc}}\geq(1-\gamma)^{-1}C_{\texttt{cov},\gamma}, and 𝒞πbase/π;β≤Closs\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi}};\beta}\leq C_{\texttt{loss}} for a parameter Closs≥|𝒴|C_{\texttt{loss}}\geq\lvert\mathcal{Y}\rvert. By Section J.1.1, Section J.1 is consistent with the assumption that πβ⋆∈Π\pi^{\star}_{\beta}\in\Pi.

{assumption}

[Margin] For all x∈supp⁡(μ)x\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu), the initial model πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} satisfies

πbase​(𝒚γ⋆​(x)∣x)≥(1+γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇)⋅πbase​(y∣x)∀y∉𝒚γ⋆​(x)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\geq{}(1+\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}})\cdot\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)\quad\forall{}y\not\in\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x) (134)

for a parameter γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇>0\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}>0.

{theorem}

Assume that πβ⋆∈Π\pi^{\star}_{\beta}\in\Pi (Section 4.2.1), and that Section 4.2.1 and Section 4.2 hold with respect to some γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1), with parameters CconcC_{\texttt{conc}}, ClossC_{\texttt{loss}}, and γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇>0\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}>0. For any δ,ρ∈(0,1)\delta,\rho\in(0,1), the DPO algorithm in Eq. 7 ensures that with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

ℙx∼μ[π^(𝒚γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ]≲1γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇​δ⋅O~(Cconc​log3⁡(Closs​|Π|​ρ−1)n+βlog(Cconc)+γ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mu}\left[\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\right]\lesssim{}\frac{1}{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}\delta}\cdot{}\widetilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{C_{\texttt{conc}}\log^{3}(C_{\texttt{loss}}\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})}{n}}+\beta\log(C_{\texttt{conc}})+\gamma\right) (135)

where O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}\left(\cdot\right) hides factors logarithmic in nn and CconcC_{\texttt{conc}} and doubly logarithmic in Π\Pi, ClossC_{\texttt{loss}}, and ρ−1\rho^{-1}.

We first state and prove some supporting technical lemmas, then proceed to the proof of Section J.1.

The next lemmas provide bounds on the tails of the self-rewards used in the algorithm.

{lemma}

Suppose β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1]. For any model π\pi, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the draw of x∼μx\sim\mu, y,y′∼πbase(⋅∣x)y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x), we have that for all s>0s>0,

ℙ[|βlog(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−βlog(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))|>log(2𝒞πbase/π;β)+s]≤exp(−s).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left\lvert\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right\rvert>\log(2\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi}};\beta})+s\right]\leq\exp\left(-s\right). (143)

=log⁡(𝔼x∼μ,y,y′∼πbase​(x)⁡[exp⁡(|β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))|)])+log⁡(δ−1)\displaystyle=\log\left(\En_{x\sim\mu,y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\exp\left(\left\lvert\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right\rvert\right)\right]\right)+\log(\delta^{-1}) (146)
≤log⁡(𝔼x∼μ,y,y′∼πbase​(x)⁡[exp⁡(β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x)))]CLOSE\displaystyle\leq{}\log\Bigg(\En_{x\sim\mu,y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\exp\left(\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right)\right] (147)
OPEN+𝔼x∼μ,y,y′∼πbase​(x)⁡[exp⁡(β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x)))])+log⁡(δ−1)\displaystyle\qquad+\En_{x\sim\mu,y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\exp\left(\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)\right)\right]\Bigg)+\log(\delta^{-1}) (148)
=log⁡(2​𝔼x∼μ,y,y′∼πbase​(x)​[exp⁡(β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x)))])+log⁡(δ−1)\displaystyle=\log\left(2\En_{x\sim\mu,y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\exp\left(\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right)\right]\right)+\log(\delta^{-1}) (149)

As long as β≤1\beta\leq{}1, by Jensen’s inequality, we can bound

≤𝔼x∼μ,y′∼πbase​(x)⁡[(𝔼y∼πbase​(x)⁡[π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x)]⋅πbase​(y′∣x)π⁡(y′∣x))β]\displaystyle\leq{}\En_{x\sim\mu,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\left(\En_{y\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right]\cdot\frac{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)^{\beta}\right] (152)
=𝔼x∼μ,y′∼πbase​(x)⁡[(πbase​(y′∣x)π⁡(y′∣x))β]\displaystyle=\En_{x\sim\mu,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x)}\left[\left(\frac{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)^{\beta}\right] (153)
=𝒞πbase/π;β,\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi}};\beta}, (154)

which proves the result. ∎

{lemma}

Let β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1]. For all models π\pi, we have

𝔼x∼μ,y,y′∼πbase(⋅∣x)[|βlog(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−βlog(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))|4]≤O(log4(𝒞πbase/π;β)+1).\displaystyle\En_{x\sim\mu,y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\left\lvert\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right\rvert^{4}\right]\leq{}O(\log^{4}(\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi}};\beta})+1). Proof of Section J.1.1. Define

X:=|β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))|.X\vcentcolon=\left\lvert\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right)\right\rvert. (156)

Set k=log⁡(2​𝒞πbase/π;β)k=\log(2\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi}};\beta}). We can bound

=4𝔼[∫0∞𝕀{X>t}t3dt]\displaystyle=4\En\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{I}\left\{X>t\right\}t^{3}dt\right] (158)
=4∫0∞ℙ[X>t]t3dt\displaystyle=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left[X>t\right]t^{3}dt (159)
≤k4+4∫k∞ℙ[X>t]t3dt\displaystyle\leq{}k^{4}+4\int_{k}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left[X>t\right]t^{3}dt (160)

=O⁡(k4+1),\displaystyle=O(k^{4}+1), (163)

where the third-to-last line uses Section J.1.1. ∎

J.1.2 Proof of Section J.1

Proof of Section J.1. For any model π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, define J⁡(π):=𝔼π⁡[log⁡πbase​(y∣x)]J(\pi)\vcentcolon={}\En_{\pi}\left[\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)\right]. Let π^∈Π\widehat{\pi}\in\Pi denote the model returned by the DPO algorithm in Eq. 21. and let r^​(x,y):=β​log⁡(π^​(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))\widehat{r}(x,y)\vcentcolon={}\beta\log\left(\frac{\widehat{\pi}(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right). By a standard argument (Huang et al., 2024), we have

π^∈arg​maxπ:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)𝔼π[r^(x,y)]−βD𝖪𝖫(π∥πbase).\displaystyle\widehat{\pi}\in\argmax_{\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})}\En_{\pi}[\widehat{r}(x,y)]-\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right). (165)

Therefore for any comparator model π⋆:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) (not necessarily in the model class Π\Pi), we have

=𝔼π⋆[r^(x,y)]−βD𝖪𝖫(π⋆∥πbase)−𝔼π^[r^(x,y)]+βD𝖪𝖫(π^∥πbase)\displaystyle=\En_{\pi^{\star}}[\widehat{r}(x,y)]-\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi^{\star}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right)-\En_{\widehat{\pi}}[\widehat{r}(x,y)]+\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right) (167)
+𝔼π⋆[r⋆(x,y)−r^(x,y)]+βD𝖪𝖫(π⋆∥πbase)+𝔼π^[r^(x,y)−r⋆(x,y)]−βD𝖪𝖫(π^∥πbase)\displaystyle\qquad+\En_{\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}(x,y)-\widehat{r}(x,y)]+\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi^{\star}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right)+\En_{\widehat{\pi}}[\widehat{r}(x,y)-r^{\star}(x,y)]-\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right) (168)
≤𝔼π⋆[r⋆(x,y)−r^(x,y)]+βD𝖪𝖫(π⋆∥πbase)+𝔼π^[r^(x,y)−r⋆(x,y)]−βD𝖪𝖫(π^∥πbase)\displaystyle\leq\En_{\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}(x,y)-\widehat{r}(x,y)]+\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi^{\star}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right)+\En_{\widehat{\pi}}[\widehat{r}(x,y)-r^{\star}(x,y)]-\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right) (169)
=𝔼π⋆,πbase⁡[Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)−Δr^​(x,y,y′)]+𝔼π^,πbase⁡[Δr^​(x,y,y′)−Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)]\displaystyle=\En_{\pi^{\star},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right]+\En_{\widehat{\pi},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right] (170)
+βD𝖪𝖫(π⋆∥πbase)−βD𝖪𝖫(π^∥πbase)\displaystyle\qquad+\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi^{\star}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right)-\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right) (171)

where the inequality uses Eq. 165. To bound the right-hand side above, we will use the following lemma, which is proven in the sequel. {lemma} For any model π\pi and any η>0\eta>0, we have that

𝔼π,πbase⁡[|Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)−Δr^​(x,y,y′)|]\displaystyle\En_{\pi,\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert\right] (172)

≲(𝒞π⋆+Cconc)1/2⋅(𝔼πbase,πbase⁡[|Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)−Δr^​(x,y,y′)|2​𝕀​{|Δr⋆|≤η,|Δr^|≤η}])1/2\displaystyle\lesssim{}(\mathcal{C}_{\pi^{\star}}+C_{\texttt{conc}})^{1/2}\cdot\left(\En_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert^{2}\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert\leq\eta,\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert\leq\eta\right\}\right]\right)^{1/2} (176)
+(𝒞π⋆+Cconc)1/2log(Closs)⋅(ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr⋆|>η]+ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr^|>η])1/4+βD𝖪𝖫(π⋆∥πbase).\displaystyle+(\mathcal{C}_{\pi^{\star}}+C_{\texttt{conc}})^{1/2}\log(C_{\texttt{loss}})\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]+\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]\right)^{1/4}+\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\pi^{\star}\,\|\,\pi_{\texttt{base}}\right). (177)

Let us overload notation and write Δπ​(x,y,y′)=β​log⁡(π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x))−β​log⁡(π⁡(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x))\Delta^{\pi}(x,y,y^{\prime})=\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid{}x)}\right)-\beta\log\left(\frac{\pi(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid{}x)}\right), so that Δπ^=Δr^\Delta^{\widehat{\pi}}=\Delta^{\widehat{r}} and Δπβ⋆=Δr⋆\Delta^{\pi^{\star}_{\beta}}=\Delta^{r^{\star}}. Since πβ⋆∈Π\pi^{\star}_{\beta}\in\Pi, the definition of π^\widehat{\pi} in Eq. 7 implies that

∑(x,y,y′)∈𝒟pref(Δπ^​(x,y,y′)−Δπβ⋆​(x,y,y′))2\displaystyle\sum_{(x,y,y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{\texttt{pref}}}\left(\Delta^{\widehat{\pi}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\pi^{\star}_{\beta}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right)^{2} ≤min⁡∑(x,y,y′)∈𝒟prefπ∈Π⁡(Δπ​(x,y,y′)−Δπβ⋆​(x,y,y′))2\displaystyle\leq{}\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{(x,y,y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{D}_{\texttt{pref}}}\left(\Delta^{\pi}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\pi^{\star}_{\beta}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right)^{2} (178)

=0.\displaystyle=0. (180)

≲Bn,ρ2​log⁡(|Π|​ρ−1)n=:εstat2.\displaystyle\lesssim{}\frac{B_{n,\rho}^{2}\log(\lvert\Pi\rvert\rho^{-1})}{n}=\vcentcolon\varepsilon_{\texttt{stat}}^{2}. (183)

≳γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇δ⋅𝔼x∼μ[𝕀{π^(𝐲γ⋆(x)∣x)≤1−δ}]−γ\displaystyle\gtrsim{}\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}\delta\cdot\En_{x\sim\mu}\left[\mathbb{I}\{\widehat{\pi}(\bm{y}^{\star}_{\gamma}(x)\mid{}x)\leq{}1-\delta\}\right]-\gamma (190)

Proof of Section J.1.2. For any η>0\eta>0, we can bound

+𝔼π,πbase[|Δr⋆(x,y,y′)−Δr^(x,y,y′)|𝕀{|Δr⋆|>η∨|Δr^|>η}].\displaystyle~~~~+\En_{\pi,\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\vee\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right\}\right]. (192)

For the second term above, we can use Cauchy-Schwarz to bound

𝔼π,πbase[|Δr⋆(x,y,y′)−Δr^(x,y,y′)|𝕀{|Δr⋆|>η∨|Δr^|>η}]\displaystyle\En_{\pi,\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\vee\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right\}\right] (193)
≤𝒞π1/2⋅(𝔼πbase,πbase[|Δr⋆(x,y,y′)−Δr^(x,y,y′)|2𝕀{|Δr⋆|>η∨|Δr^|>η}])1/2\displaystyle\leq{}\mathcal{C}_{\pi}^{1/2}\cdot\left(\En_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert^{2}\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\vee\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right\}\right]\right)^{1/2} (194)
≲𝒞π1/2⋅(ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr⋆|>η]+ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr^|>η])1/4\displaystyle\lesssim{}\mathcal{C}_{\pi}^{1/2}\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]+\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]\right)^{1/4} (195)
⋅(𝔼πbase,πbase⁡[|Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)|4]+𝔼πbase,πbase⁡[|Δr^​(x,y,y′)|4])1/4\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\cdot{}\left(\En_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert^{4}\right]+\En_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert^{4}\right]\right)^{1/4} (196)
≲𝒞π1/2⋅(ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr⋆|>η]+ℙπbase,πbase[|Δr^|>η])1/4⋅(log(𝒞πbase/π^;β)+log(𝒞πbase/πβ⋆;β)),\displaystyle\lesssim{}\mathcal{C}_{\pi}^{1/2}\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]+\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert>\eta\right]\right)^{1/4}\cdot{}(\log(\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\widehat{\pi}}};\beta})+\log(\mathcal{C}_{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}}{{\pi^{\star}_{\beta}}};\beta})), (197)

where the last inequality follows from Section J.1.1.

Meanwhile, for the first term, for any λ>0\lambda>0 we can bound

𝔼π,πbase⁡[|Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)−Δr^​(x,y,y′)|​𝕀​{|Δr⋆|≤η,|Δr^|≤η}]\displaystyle\En_{\pi,\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert\leq\eta,\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert\leq\eta\right\}\right] (198)
≤𝒞π1/2​(𝔼πbase,πbase⁡[|Δr⋆​(x,y,y′)−Δr^​(x,y,y′)|2​𝕀​{|Δr⋆|≤η,|Δr^|≤η}])1/2.\displaystyle\leq{}\mathcal{C}_{\pi}^{1/2}\left(\En_{\pi_{\texttt{base}},\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\left[\left\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}(x,y,y^{\prime})-\Delta^{\widehat{r}}(x,y,y^{\prime})\right\rvert^{2}\mathbb{I}\left\{\big\lvert\Delta^{r^{\star}}\big\rvert\leq\eta,\big\lvert\Delta^{\widehat{r}}\big\rvert\leq\eta\right\}\right]\right)^{1/2}. (199)

∎

J.2 Proof of Section 4.2.2 and Section 4.2.2

In this section we prove Section 4.2.2 as well as Section 4.2.2, the application to linear softmax models. For the formal theorem statements, see Section J.2.3 and Section J.2.4 respectively. The section is organized as follows.

  • •

    Section J.2.1 gives necessary background on KL-regularized policy optimization, as well as the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient.

  • •

    Section J.2.2 presents a generic guarantee for XPO under a general choice of reward function.

  • •

    Section J.2.3 instantiates the result above with the self-reward function r⁡(x,y):=log⁡πbase​(y∣x)r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x) to prove Section 4.2.2.

  • •

    Finally, Section J.2.4 applies the preceding results to prove Section 4.2.2.

J.2.1 Background

To begin, we give background on KL-regularized policy optimization and the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient.

KL-regularized policy optimization

Let β>0\beta>0 be given, and let r:𝒳×𝒴→[−R𝗆𝖺𝗑,R𝗆𝖺𝗑]r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-R_{\mathsf{max}},R_{\mathsf{max}}] be an unknown reward function on prompt/action pairs. Define a value function JβJ_{\beta} over model class Π\Pi by:

Jβ(π):=𝔼π[r(x,y)]−β⋅D𝖪𝖫(ℙπ∥ℙπbase).\displaystyle J_{\beta}(\pi):=\En_{\pi}[r(x,y)]-\beta\cdot D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\mathbb{P}^{\pi}\,\|\,\mathbb{P}^{\pi_{\texttt{base}}}\right). (200)

We refer to this as a KL-regularized policy optimization objective (we use the term “policy” following the reinforcement learning literature; for our setting, policies correspond to models). Given query access to rr, the goal is to find π^∈Π\widehat{\pi}\in\Pi such that

Jβ​(πβ⋆)−Jβ​(π^)≤ϵ\displaystyle J_{\beta}(\pi^{\star}_{\beta})-J_{\beta}(\widehat{\pi})\leq\epsilon (201)

where πβ⋆​(y∣x)∝πbase​(y∣x)​exp⁡(β−1​r​(x,y))\pi^{\star}_{\beta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\exp(\beta^{-1}r(x,y)) is the model that maximizes JβJ_{\beta} over all models π:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}).

We make use of the following assumptions, as in Xie et al. (2024).

{assumption}

[Realizability] It holds that πβ⋆∈Π\pi^{\star}_{\beta}\in\Pi.

{assumption}

[Bounded density ratios] For all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, |β​log⁡π⁡(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x)|≤V𝗆𝖺𝗑\big\lvert\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)}\big\rvert\leq V_{\mathsf{max}}.

Finally, we require two definitions.

{definition}

[Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient for RLHF, (Xie et al., 2024)] For a model class Π\Pi, reward function rr, reference model πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}}, and parameters T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} and β,λ>0\beta,\lambda>0, the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient is defined as

𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π,r,T,β,λ,πbase)\displaystyle\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi,r,T,\beta,\lambda;\pi_{\texttt{base}}) (202)
:=supπ(1),…,π(T)∈Π{∑t=1T𝔼(t)​[β​log⁡π(t)​(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x)−r⁡(x,y)−β​log⁡π(t)​(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x)+r⁡(x,y′)]2λ∨∑i=1t−1𝔼(i)​[(β​log⁡π(t)​(y∣x)πbase​(y∣x)−r⁡(x,y)−β​log⁡π(t)​(y′∣x)πbase​(y′∣x)+r⁡(x,y′))2]}\displaystyle:=\sup_{\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]}\right\} (203)

where 𝔼(t)\mathbb{E}^{(t)} denotes expectation over x∼μx\sim\mu, y∼π(t)(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi^{(t)}(\cdot\mid x), and y′∼πbase(⋅∣x)y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\cdot\mid x).

{definition}

Let ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We say that Ψ⊆Π\Psi\subseteq\Pi is a ϵ\epsilon-net for model class Π\Pi if for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi there exists π′∈Ψ\pi^{\prime}\in\Psi such that

maxx∈𝒳⁡maxy∈𝒴​|log⁡π⁡(y∣x)π′​(y∣x)|≤ϵ.\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left|\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\prime}(y\mid x)}\right|\leq\epsilon. (204)

We write 𝒩⁡(Π,ϵ)\mathcal{N}(\Pi,\epsilon) to denote the size of the smallest ϵ\epsilon-net for Π\Pi.

J.2.2 Guarantees for KL-regularized policy optimization with XPO

In this section, we give self-contained guarantees for the XPO algorithm (Algorithm 1). XPO was introduced in Xie et al. (2024) for KL-regularized policy optimization in the related setting where the learner only has indirect access to the reward function rr through preference data (specifically, pairs of actions labeled via a Bradley-Terry model). Standard offline algorithms for this problem, such as DPO, require bounds on concentrability of the model class (see e.g. Eq. 22). Xie et al. (2024) show that the XPO algorithm avoids this dependence, and instead requires bounded Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient.

Algorithm 1 is a variant of the XPO algorithm which is adapted to reward-based feedback (as opposed to preference-based feedback), and Section J.2.2 shows that this algorithm enjoys guarantees similar to those of Xie et al. (2024) for this setting. Note that this is not an immediate corollary of the results in Xie et al. (2024), since the sample complexity in the preference-based setting scales with eO⁡(R𝗆𝖺𝗑)e^{O(R_{\mathsf{max}})}, and for our application to sharpening it is important to avoid this dependence. However, our algorithm and analysis only diverge from Xie et al. (2024) in a few places.

{theorem}

[Variant of Xie et al. (2024, Theorem 3.1)] Suppose that Sections J.2.1 and J.2.1 hold. For any T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}, ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼,ρ∈(0,1)\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}},\rho\in(0,1), by setting α:=βR𝗆𝖺𝗑+V𝗆𝖺𝗑​log⁡(2​𝒩​(Π,ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)​T/ρ)𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π)​T\alpha:=\frac{\beta}{R_{\mathsf{max}}+V_{\mathsf{max}}}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2\mathcal{N}(\Pi,\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})T/\rho)}{\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi)T}}, Algorithm 1 produces a model π^∈Π\widehat{\pi}\in\Pi such that with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

βD𝖪𝖫(π^∥πβ⋆)=Jβ(πβ⋆)−Jβ(π^)\displaystyle\beta D_{\mathsf{KL}}\left(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\beta}\right)=J_{\beta}(\pi^{\star}_{\beta})-J_{\beta}(\widehat{\pi}) ≲(R𝗆𝖺𝗑+V𝗆𝖺𝗑)​𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π)​log⁡(2​𝒩​(Π,ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)​T/ρ)T\displaystyle\lesssim(R_{\mathsf{max}}+V_{\mathsf{max}})\sqrt{\frac{\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi)\log(2\mathcal{N}(\Pi,\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})T/\rho)}{T}} (207)
+β​ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼​𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π)​T\displaystyle+\beta\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}\sqrt{\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi)T} (208)

where 𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π):=𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Π,r,T,β,V𝗆𝖺𝗑2,πbase)\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi):=\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi,r,T,\beta,V_{\mathsf{max}}^{2};\pi_{\texttt{base}}).

where 𝒟(t)\mathcal{D}^{(t)} is the dataset defined in iteration tt of Algorithm 1. J.2.4 Application: linear softmax models

In this section we apply Section 4.2.2 to the class of linear softmax models, proving Section 4.2.2. This demonstrates that Algorithm 1 can achieve an exponential improvement in sample complexity compared to SFT-Sharpening.

{definition}

[Linear softmax model] Let d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} be given, and let ϕ:𝒳×𝒴→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a feature map with ∥ϕ⁡(x,y)∥2≤1\lVert\phi(x,y)\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for all x,yx,y. Let π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) be the uniform model π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​(y∣x):=1|𝒴|\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}, and let B≥1B\geq 1.1515 15 We use the notation π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈\pi_{\mathsf{zero}} to highlight the fact that π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈=πθ\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}=\pi_{\theta} for θ=0\theta=0. We consider the linear softmax model class Πϕ,B:={πθ:θ∈ℝd,∥θ∥2≤B}\Pi_{\phi,B}:=\{\pi_{\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B\} where πθ:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒴)\pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) is defined by

πθ​(y∣x)∝π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​(y∣x)​exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x,y),θ⟩).\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle). (245)
{theorem}

[Restatement of Section 4.2.2] Let ϵ,δ,γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇,ρ∈(0,1)\epsilon,\delta,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}},\rho\in(0,1) be given. Suppose that πbase=πθ⋆∈Πϕ,B\pi_{\texttt{base}}=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B} for some θ⋆∈ℝd\theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥θ⋆∥2≤γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇​B3​log⁡(2​|𝒴|/δ)\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}B}{3\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)}. Also, suppose that πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} satisfies Section 4.2 with parameter γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}. Then Algorithm 1 with base model πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}}, reward function r⁡(x,y):=log⁡πbase​(x,y)r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(x,y), regularization parameter β:=γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇/(2​log⁡(2​|𝒴|/δ))\beta:=\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}/(2\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)), and optimism parameter α⁡(T)∝βB+log⁡(|𝒴|)​d​log⁡(B​d​T/(ϵ​δ))+log⁡(T/ρ)d​T​log⁡(T)\alpha(T)\propto\frac{\beta}{B+\log(|\mathcal{Y}|)}\sqrt{\frac{d\log(BdT/(\epsilon\delta))+\log(T/\rho)}{dT\log(T)}} returns an (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-sharpened model with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho, and has sample complexity

m=poly⁡(ϵ−1,δ−1,γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇−1,d,B,log⁡(|𝒴|/ρ)).m=\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1},\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},d,B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|/\rho)). (246)

Before proving the result, we unpack the conditions. Section J.2.4 requires the base model πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} to lie in the model class and also satisfy the margin condition (Section 4.2). For any constant ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0, the sharpening algorithm then succeeds with sample complexity poly⁡(d,γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇−1,B,log⁡(|𝒴|))\mathrm{poly}(d,\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}^{-1},B,\log(|\mathcal{Y}|)). These conditions are non-vacuous; in fact, there are fairly natural examples for which non-exploratory algorithm such as SFT-Sharpening require sample complexity exp⁡(Ω⁡(d))\exp(\Omega(d)), whereas all of the above parameters are poly⁡(d)\mathrm{poly}(d). The following is one such example.

{example}

[Separation between RLHF-Sharpening and SFT-Sharpening ] Set 𝒳={x}\mathcal{X}=\{x\} and let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a 1/41/4-packing of the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} of cardinality exp⁡(Θ⁡(d))\exp(\Theta(d)). Define ϕ:𝒳×𝒴→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} by ϕ⁡(x,y):=y\phi(x,y):=y, and let B=C​d​log⁡dB=Cd\log d for an absolute constant C>0C>0. Fix any y⋆∈𝒴y^{\star}\in\mathcal{Y} and define πbase:=πθ⋆∈Πϕ,B\pi_{\texttt{base}}:=\pi_{\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B} by θ⋆:=y⋆\theta^{\star}:=y^{\star}. Then for any y≠y⋆y\neq y^{\star}, we have ⟨y,y⋆⟩≤1−Ω⁡(1)\langle y,y^{\star}\rangle\leq 1-\Omega(1), so

πbase​(y⋆∣x)πbase​(y∣x)=exp⁡(⟨y⋆−y,y⋆⟩)=exp⁡(Ω⁡(1))=1+Ω⁡(1).\frac{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)}=\exp(\langle y^{\star}-y,y^{\star}\rangle)=\exp(\Omega(1))=1+\Omega(1). (247)

Thus, πbase\pi_{\texttt{base}} satisfies Section 4.2 with γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇=Ω⁡(1)\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}=\Omega(1). Moreover, ∥θ⋆∥2=1≤γ𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇​B3​log⁡(2​|𝒴|/δ)\lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}=1\leq\frac{\gamma_{\mathsf{margin}}B}{3\log(2|\mathcal{Y}|/\delta)} for any δ=1/poly⁡(d)\delta=1/\mathrm{poly}(d), so long as CC is a sufficiently large constant. It follows from Section 4.2.2 that Algorithm 1 computes an (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-sharpened model with sample complexity poly⁡(ϵ−1,δ−1,d)\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1},d). However, since πbase​(y⋆∣x)≤πbase​(y∣x)⋅exp⁡(2)\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)\leq\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)\cdot\exp(2) for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, it is clear that

Ccov=𝔼⁡[1πbase​(𝒚⋆​(x)∣x)]=1πbase​(y⋆∣x)=Ω⁡(|𝒴|)=exp⁡(Ω⁡(d)).C_{\texttt{cov}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(\bm{y}^{\star}(x)\mid x)}\right]=\frac{1}{\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y^{\star}\mid x)}=\Omega(|\mathcal{Y}|)=\exp(\Omega(d)). (248)

Thus, the sample complexity guarantee for SFT-Sharpening in Section 4.1 will incur exponential dependence on dd in the sample complexity. It is straightforward to check that this dependence is real for SFT-Sharpening, and not just an artifact of the analysis, since the model that SFT-Sharpening is trying to learn (via MLE) will itself not be sharp in this example, unless exp⁡(Ω⁡(d))\exp(\Omega(d)) samples are drawn per prompt.

We now proceed to the proof of Section J.2.4, which requires the following bounds on the covering number and the Sequential Extrapolation Coefficient of Πϕ,B\Pi_{\phi,B}.

{lemma}

Let ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼>0\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}>0. Then Πϕ,B\Pi_{\phi,B} has an ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}-net of size (6​B/ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)d(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}.

Proof of Section J.2.4. By a standard packing argument, there is a set {θ1,…,θN}\{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}\} of size (6​B/ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)d(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d} such that for every θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥θ∥2≤B\lVert\theta\rVert_{2}\leq B there is some i∈[N]i\in[N] with ∥θi−θ∥2≤ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2\lVert\theta_{i}-\theta\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2. Now for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

log⁡πθ​(y∣x)πθi​(y∣x)\displaystyle\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y\mid x)} =log⁡exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x,y),θ⟩)exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x,y),θi⟩)+log⁡𝔼(x′,y′)∼π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​exp​(⟨ϕ⁡(x′,y′),θi⟩)𝔼(x′,y′)∼π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​exp​(⟨ϕ⁡(x′,y′),θ⟩)\displaystyle=\log\frac{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta\rangle)}{\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta_{i}\rangle)}+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}\rangle)}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)} (249)
=⟨ϕ⁡(x,y),θ−θi⟩+log⁡𝔼(x′,y′)∼π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈[exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x′,y′),θ⟩)​exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x′,y′),θi−θ⟩)]𝔼(x′,y′)∼π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​exp​(⟨ϕ⁡(x′,y′),θ⟩).\displaystyle=\langle\phi(x,y),\theta-\theta_{i}\rangle+\log\frac{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\left[\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}-\theta\rangle)\right]}{\E_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}}\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta\rangle)}. (250)

The first term is bounded by ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2 in magnitude. In the second term, we have exp(⟨ϕ(x′,y′),θi−θ⟩)∈[exp(−ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2),exp(ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2)]\exp(\langle\phi(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\theta_{i}-\theta\rangle)\in[\exp(-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2),\exp(\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2)], so the ratio of expectations lies in [exp(−ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2),exp(ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2)][\exp(-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2),\exp(\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2)] as well, and so the log-ratio lies in [−ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2,ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼/2][-\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2,\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}/2]. In all, we get |log⁡πθ​(y|x)πθi​(y∣x)|≤ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼\left|\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y\mid x)}\right|\leq\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}. Thus, {πθ1,…,πθN}\{\pi_{\theta_{1}},\dots,\pi_{\theta_{N}}\} is an ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}}-net for Π\Pi. ∎

{lemma}

Let r:𝒳×𝒴→[−R𝗆𝖺𝗑,R𝗆𝖺𝗑]r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-R_{\mathsf{max}},R_{\mathsf{max}}] be a reward function and let T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} and β>0\beta>0. If λ≥4​β2​B2+R𝗆𝖺𝗑2\lambda\geq 4\beta^{2}B^{2}+R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2} then for any π⋆∈Πϕ,B\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\phi,B},

𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Πϕ,B,r,T,β,λ,π⋆)≲d​log⁡(T+1).\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,\lambda;\pi^{\star})\lesssim d\log(T+1). (251)

Proof of Section J.2.4. Fix π(1),…,π(T)∈Πϕ,B.\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}. By definition, there are some θ(1),…,θ(T)∈ℝd\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(T)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥θ(t)∥2≤B\lVert\theta^{(t)}\rVert_{2}\leq B and

π(t)​(y∣x)∝π𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈​(y∣x)​exp⁡(⟨ϕ⁡(x,y),θ(t)⟩)\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathsf{zero}}(y\mid x)\exp(\langle\phi(x,y),\theta^{(t)}\rangle) (252)

for all t∈[T]t\in[T] and (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. Then for any t∈[T]t\in[T] we have

𝔼(t)​[β​log⁡π(t)​(y∣x)π⋆​(y∣x)−r⁡(x,y)−β​log⁡π(t)​(y′∣x)π⋆​(y′∣x)+r⁡(x,y′)]2λ∨∑i=1t−1𝔼(i)​[(β​log⁡π(t)​(y∣x)π⋆​(y∣x)−r⁡(x,y)−β​log⁡π(t)​(y′∣x)π⋆​(y′∣x)+r⁡(x,y′))2]\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)}-r(x,y)-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{(t)}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi^{\star}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}+r(x,y^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]} (253)
=𝔼(t)​[⟨ϕ~​(x,y)−ϕ~​(x,y′),θ~(t)⟩]2λ∨∑i=1t−1𝔼(i)​[(⟨ϕ~​(x,y)−ϕ~​(x,y′),θ~(t)⟩)2]\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}^{(t)}\left[\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right]^{2}}{\lambda\lor\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[\left(\langle\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}),\widetilde{\theta}^{(t)}\rangle\right)^{2}\right]} (254)

where for each i∈[T]i\in[T] we have defined Σ(i):=𝔼(i)​[(ϕ~​(x,y)−ϕ~​(x,y′))​(ϕ~​(x,y)−ϕ~​(x,y′))⊤]\Sigma^{(i)}:=\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\left[(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))(\widetilde{\phi}(x,y)-\widetilde{\phi}(x,y^{\prime}))^{\top}\right]. Since π(1),…,π(T)∈Π\pi^{(1)},\dots,\pi^{(T)}\in\Pi were arbitrary, this completes the proof. ∎

The proof is now immediate from Section J.2.3 and the above lemmas.

Proof of Section J.2.4. By the assumption on θ⋆\theta^{\star} and choice of β\beta, the model πβ⋆\pi^{\star}_{\beta} defined by πβ⋆​(y∣x)∝πbase​(y∣x)1+β−1\pi^{\star}_{\beta}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x)^{1+\beta^{-1}} satisfies πβ⋆=π(1+β−1)​θ⋆∈Πϕ,B\pi^{\star}_{\beta}=\pi_{(1+\beta^{-1})\theta^{\star}}\in\Pi_{\phi,B}. By Section J.2.4, we have 𝒩⁡(Πϕ,B,ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)≤(6​B/ϵ𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼)d\mathcal{N}(\Pi_{\phi,B},\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})\leq(6B/\epsilon_{\mathsf{disc}})^{d}. Take R𝗆𝖺𝗑:=4​β2​B2+(2​B+log⁡|𝒴|)2R_{\mathsf{max}}:=\sqrt{4\beta^{2}B^{2}+(2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|)^{2}}. We know that r⁡(x,y):=log⁡πbase​(y∣x)r(x,y):=\log\pi_{\texttt{base}}(y\mid x) satisfies |r⁡(x,y)|≤2​B+log⁡|𝒴||r(x,y)|\leq 2B+\log|\mathcal{Y}| for all x,yx,y. By Section J.2.4, we therefore get that 𝖲𝖤𝖢⁡(Πϕ,B,r,T,β,R𝗆𝖺𝗑2,πbase)≲d​log⁡(T+1)\mathsf{SEC}(\Pi_{\phi,B},r,T,\beta,R_{\mathsf{max}}^{2};\pi_{\texttt{base}})\lesssim d\log(T+1). Substituting these bounds into Section J.2.3 yields the claimed result. ∎
